newsitem.title: USA: NYC says break on clothing tax boosted sales.
newsitem.headline: NYC says break on clothing tax boosted sales.

text.p: New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, who has been urging Albany to phase-out sales taxes on clothing that costs less than $500, said a one-week experiment led to big gains in sales, boosting his plan.
The city, like most localities through-out the state, had joined the state in offering shoppers a one-week moratorium on such taxes that ran from January 18 to January 24.

New York City shoppers, who pay a total of eight percent in state and city sales taxes plus a 0.25 percent levy for the Metropolitan Transportation Authority, much higher rates than paid by residents in nearby states, evidently responded with enthusiasm though direct comparisons are difficult as last year's data was skewed by poor weather that dampened interest.

At a news conference at the Manhattan Mall in midtown, where store managers estimated sales rose 40 percent to 400 percent, Giuliani released estimates showing that eliminating the tax could create 17,400 jobs and pump $1.2 billion of direct and indirect spending into the city's economy.

"As real numbers become available, we are learning that last week's sales were even better than expected," Giuliani said, in prepared remarks. Economists have said a one-week period is too brief for drawing firm conclusions.
Gov George Pataki, a Republican, has said that while he supported eliminating the state's four-percent sales tax on clothing that costs less than $500, it would be hard to do this year.
The governor has proposed a number of other tax breaks in his fiscal 1998 budget, including ones on estate and gift taxes.

The mayor could start the 1998 fiscal year on July 1 with an approximately $350 million surplus, mainly due to a banner year by Wall Street powerhouses, and is expected to propose using the funds to help close outyear budget gaps and cut taxes, the New York Post said on Monday.
Giuliani's preliminary budget for fiscal 1998 is due on January 30, and there has been speculation that the tax reductions would include phasing out the city's four-percent sales tax.
"There's every indication that's what it is going to be, that's the rumor," said a city source, who declined to be named.
Albany lawmakers would have to approve such a step, and a spokeswoman for the mayor was not immediately available to comment.
